# Saturated fixed-facet cuts: an exact two-rate feasibility test

This note extends the proper-cut two-rate certificate to all endpoint-cut
statuses. It uses the scalar quantile meeting-point construction in
`candidate 09edc6fea46c7827`.
The test below is necessary and sufficient for strict first-order decrease
of this particular finite-menu upper certificate. It is not a necessary
condition for arbitrary deformations, and no geometric inequality forcing
the test is asserted.

## 1. Actual bodies, one tied endpoint, and nested deformations

Let d>=1. Let A,K,B be d-dimensional convex bodies, at integer bases
-1,0,1, with (A+B)/2 subset K. Write

    a=|A|, k=|K|, b=|B|, M=a+k+b.

Let v_0,...,v_d span R^d and have sole linear dependence sum_i v_i=0.
Let y0 belong to int K, h_i=h_B(v_i), and beta_i=2v_i.y0-h_i.
Assume the actual through-source caps

    v_i.(x-y0)+(v_i.y0-h_i)z >= 0

have common raw volume Q, and Q is the true global maximal raw depth.
Their B traces are support faces and have zero d-volume. Put

    U_i=|A intersect {v_i.x>=beta_i}|,
    r=Q/M.

Let m_A,m_B be the maximum ordinary raw depths of the endpoint bodies.
Assume m_A<Q and m_B=Q. Their actual mixed depths equal these ordinary
depths: a steep finite integer tilt can isolate either endpoint at any
specified continuous threshold, since all three bodies are bounded.

Fix actual contraction centers p in A and q in B. For rates u,v>=0,
not both zero, set

    A_t=p+(1-ut)(A-p), B_t=q+(1-vt)(B-q), K_t=K.              (1)

For small t>=0 these are positive-volume nested bodies, so compatibility
persists. Set

    c_i=beta_i-v_i.p, e_i=h_i-v_i.q>=0.

The new B support is h_i-tv e_i. Retain the v_i and this exact support.
The scalar functions

    f_i(s,t)=|K intersect {v_i.x>=s}|
           +|A_t intersect {v_i.x>=2s-h_i+tv e_i}|

are strictly decreasing near s_i0=v_i.y0, with a uniform positive slope
bound from the proper K section. The quantile argument therefore gives
a unique nearby common budget q_menu(t) and one nearby meeting point
y(t) in int K. All its displayed caps have budget q_menu(t). Their
middle traces cover R^d, since sum_i v_i=0. Hence they bound the raw
depth of EVERY point in the middle fiber by q_menu(t).

The quantile existence, O(t) estimates, and one-sided differentiation
proof in the cited source apply unchanged: the support displacement is
linear in t, and the A indicator changes in L1 by O(t). For completeness,
the exact first-order equations and their unique solution are established
next; thus no differentiability of a saturated volume function is assumed.

## 2. Scalar responses and their explicit inverses

Let k_i>0 denote the normalized K section measure at s_i0. Let sigma_i
be the normalized A section measure at beta_i: the ordinary section for
a proper cut, the limiting support-face measure at either endpoint, and
zero for an exterior threshold. A support face of dimension less than
d-1 has sigma_i=0. In d=1 the normalized supporting singleton has the
usual H_0 measure divided by ||v_i||. Define

    psi_i(x)=x       for a proper A cut,
             x_+     for a full A cut at its minimum support,
             min(x,0) for an empty A cut at its maximum support,
             0       for a strict exterior cut.                    (2)

The exterior case has sigma_i=0. For bounded source velocity z_i,
homothety pulls the A threshold back to

    beta_i+t(2z_i+u c_i+v e_i)+O(t^2).

Proper section continuity and the one-sided support-section limits give
the uniform first-order menu response

    R_i(z_i;u,v)=-k_i z_i-duU_i
                 -sigma_i psi_i(2z_i+u c_i+v e_i).                 (3)

The limiting support-section formula includes full and empty cuts with
facets. For instance, a full cut at minimum support loses du a plus
sigma_i times the positive part of the threshold displacement; an empty
cut at maximum support gains sigma_i times its negative part. These are
exact first-order responses, not free choices of fractional sections.

Each R_i is continuous, strictly decreasing onto R. Write the common
menu loss as L=-q_menu'(0). Solving R_i(z_i;u,v)=-L gives

    H_i(L;u,v)=2L-2duU_i+k_i(u c_i+v e_i),

    Z_i(L;u,v)=(L-duU_i)/k_i
       -sigma_i/[k_i(k_i+2sigma_i)] psi_i(H_i(L;u,v)).             (4)

To check (4), on an active proper or hinge branch the solution is

    z_i=[L-duU_i-sigma_i(u c_i+v e_i)]/(k_i+2sigma_i).

Its hinge argument has the sign of H_i. On an inactive branch it is
(L-duU_i)/k_i, and its hinge argument again has the sign of H_i. Thus
the branch choice in (4) is exactly consistent.

Define Phi(L;u,v)=sum_i Z_i(L;u,v). It is continuous, strictly increasing
onto R, with slopes between sum_i 1/(k_i+2sigma_i) and sum_i 1/k_i.
The common source velocity must satisfy sum_i z_i=0. Consequently L is
the UNIQUE solution

    Phi(L;u,v)=0.                                                  (5)

The O(t) quantile estimates make the difference quotients bounded.
Every convergent subsequence solves (3),(5), by the uniform expansion;
uniqueness proves convergence of all difference quotients. This proves
existence of the actual right derivatives used above. Positive
homogeneity of (4) also gives L(hu,hv)=hL(u,v) for h>=0.

## 3. Exact strict first-order certificate

The actual new global maximum is bounded above by

    max{(1-ut)^d m_A, (1-vt)^d Q, q_menu(t)}.                      (6)

The first term retains a strict gap. The total mass has derivative
-d(au+bv). Thus BOTH remaining normalized upper bounds strictly decrease
to first order exactly when

    L(u,v)>dr(au+bv),
    Qv>r(au+bv).                                                   (7)

For u>0 put tau=v/u. The second inequality is exactly

    tau>tau0:=a/(a+k).                                            (8)

Because Phi is strictly increasing, the first inequality in (7) is
equivalent to

    Psi(tau):=Phi(dr(a+b tau);1,tau)<0.                            (9)

This is a directly evaluable test at a specified trial loss, without
solving for the actual loss or selecting any theta independently.

## 4. Concavity removes the search over all rate ratios

At the trial loss in (9), the hinge argument is

    H_i=A_i+B_i tau,
    A_i=2dra-2dU_i+k_i c_i,
    B_i=2drb+k_i e_i>0.                                           (10)

For an empty A cut, U_i=0 and c_i>=0. Thus H_i>0 for tau>=0,
because r,a>0; its negative-part hinge in (2) is identically zero.
Proper cuts contribute affine functions. Full-at-minimum cuts contribute
a negative multiple of (A_i+B_i tau)_+. Strict exterior cuts contribute
affine functions. Therefore Psi is a continuous CONCAVE piecewise-affine
function on [0,infinity). This is the relevant monotonicity: its slopes
are nonincreasing. It does not assert that the actual loss is linear.

For a full-at-minimum cut, U_i=a, c_i<=0, and r<1, so A_i<0; its
only possible breakpoint is the positive number -A_i/B_i. There are
finitely many such breakpoints. Beyond all of them, the slope is

    S_infinity=W_infinity(drb-J_infinity),                         (11)

where

    theta_i^infinity=1 for proper or full-at-minimum cuts,
                      0 for empty or strict exterior cuts,
    w_i^infinity=1/(k_i+2theta_i^infinity sigma_i),
    W_infinity=sum_i w_i^infinity,
    J_infinity=sum_i w_i^infinity theta_i^infinity sigma_i e_i
                    /W_infinity.                                (12)

Terms with sigma_i=0 are independent of their theta label.

A concave piecewise-affine function with finitely many breakpoints is
negative somewhere on (tau0,infinity) if and only if either its value
at tau0 is strictly negative or its eventual slope is strictly negative.
Indeed either condition suffices by continuity or eventual linearity.
Conversely, if the initial value and eventual slope are both nonnegative,
every earlier slope is nonnegative by concavity, so the function never
falls below its initial value.

We have proved the EXACT feasibility criterion

    Psi(tau0)<0  OR  J_infinity>drb.                              (13)

The second alternative is also precisely the B-only criterion u=0,v=1:
at trial loss drb every nonempty hinge has positive argument, so
Phi(drb;0,1)=W_infinity(drb-J_infinity). The tied endpoint's own
normalized depth strictly decreases for B-only contraction, since
Q>rb. Thus this alternative needs no limiting infinite rate.

If the first alternative holds, continuity supplies an actual finite
ratio tau>tau0 for which both tests in (7) hold. If neither alternative
holds, no nonnegative rates satisfy the two strict first-order tests.
Zero first derivatives may require higher-order information; this note
makes no claim about them.

## 5. One finite boundary calculation and the proper-cut specialization

By homogeneity, the first alternative in (13) is equivalently

    Phi(daQ;a+k,a)<0.                                             (14)

This is often a convenient calculation. Set

    H_i^*=2daQ-2d(a+k)U_i+k_i[(a+k)c_i+a e_i].

Take theta_i^*=1 for proper cuts, 0 for empty cuts or strict exteriors,
and for full-at-minimum cuts take 1 if H_i^*>0, 0 if H_i^*<0, and either
value if H_i^*=0. Then the left side of (14) is exactly

    sum_i [daQ-d(a+k)U_i
            -theta_i^* sigma_i((a+k)c_i+a e_i)]
                 /(k_i+2theta_i^* sigma_i).                       (15)

These theta values are dictated by a known trial target and actual
geometry. They are not optimization variables. At a zero argument both
branches in (15) agree.

If all A cuts are proper, define fixed weights w_i=1/(k_i+2sigma_i)
and their weighted means

    Lbar=sum_i w_i(dU_i+sigma_i c_i)/sum_i w_i,
    Jbar=sum_i w_i sigma_i e_i/sum_i w_i.

Then (13) reduces exactly to

    Jbar>drb  OR  (a+k)Lbar+a Jbar>daQ,                            (16)

recovering the former planar test when d=2. In the saturated case the
boundary weights in (15) can differ from the B-only weights in (12);
replacing both by freely optimized or common weights would be invalid.

All assertions above retain one actual pair of contraction centers p,q.
The criterion may be evaluated for any such pair. No assertion is made
that independent support maxima can be combined when their hinge-selected
weights differ, or that a pair satisfying (13) must always exist.

## 6. Exact finite support-function optimization of the actual centers

One can nevertheless optimize (13) over p in A and q in B exactly,
without ever pretending that arbitrary theta values are actual derivative
weights. The reason is a lower-envelope identity specific to the trial
target, where the empty-cut branches have already become inactive.

Let Theta be the finite set of choices theta_i=1 on proper cuts, theta_i=0
on empty and strict exterior cuts, and theta_i in {0,1} independently
on full-at-minimum cuts. For a fixed theta in Theta put

    w_i^theta=1/(k_i+2theta_i sigma_i), W_theta=sum_i w_i^theta,
    V_theta=sum_i w_i^theta theta_i sigma_i v_i,

    C_theta=daQ W_theta-d(a+k)sum_i w_i^theta U_i
       -sum_i w_i^theta theta_i sigma_i[(a+k)beta_i+a h_i].         (17)

Then the boundary trial sum satisfies the EXACT identity

    Phi(daQ;a+k,a)
      =min_(theta in Theta){C_theta+(a+k)V_theta.p+a V_theta.q}.   (18)

Indeed for a full-at-minimum cut the inverse in (4) is the minimum
of its inactive value (L-du a)/k_i and its active value
[L-du a-sigma_i(uc_i+ve_i)]/(k_i+2sigma_i). Their difference is
-sigma_i H_i/[k_i(k_i+2sigma_i)], so their lower envelope is exactly
the required positive-part hinge. The minimum of a sum of these finitely
many independent two-branch terms equals the minimum over Theta. Proper
terms have one branch and empty terms have the already proved inactive
branch. Expanding c_i,e_i yields (18).

Since Theta is finite and A,B are compact, both sides have attained
minima over the actual contraction centers. Therefore

    min_(p in A,q in B) Phi(daQ;a+k,a)
      =min_(theta in Theta)
          {C_theta-(a+k)h_A(-V_theta)-a h_B(-V_theta)}.             (19)

Each displayed support minimum uses one actual p and one actual q in
their respective bodies, with the SAME vector -V_theta. If a selected
branch is not active at those support points, the actual Phi is no
larger by (18), so strict negativity is preserved. Conversely, any
negative actual Phi has an active branch giving that same negative
value. Thus (19) creates no unsupported claim of selectable response
weights; it optimizes a proven finite lower envelope.

The B-only alternative has fixed infinity weights (12). Its attained
maximum over q in B is

    J_infinity^max=
       [sum_i w_i^infinity theta_i^infinity sigma_i h_i
                         +h_B(-V_infinity)]/W_infinity,           (20)

where V_infinity=sum_i w_i^infinity theta_i^infinity sigma_i v_i.

Consequently there exist actual centers and nonnegative contraction
rates making BOTH normalized bounds in (7) strictly decrease if and
only if either the right side of (19) is strictly negative or

    J_infinity^max>drb.                                          (21)

This is a finite exact criterion involving the actual cap volumes,
actual section densities, and actual support functions. It does not
assert that the criterion holds for every critical configuration.

## 7. Exact empty-status preservation and the loss envelope

For these nested two-endpoint contractions, initially empty A cuts in
fact remain empty at the actual meeting point for all sufficiently
small t>=0. At every initial level s_i0, the new A set is smaller and
its threshold has increased by tv e_i>=0, so f_i(s_i0,t)<=Q. The inverse
quantile at Q is therefore at most s_i0 for every i. Their sum is
nonpositive, which forces q_menu(t)<=Q by strict monotonicity of the
sum of inverses. For an initially empty A cut the equality
f_i(s_i0,t)=Q holds exactly: its A trace is still empty in volume and
its K cap is unchanged. Consequently its meeting level for
q_menu(t)<=Q is at least s_i0. Its actual A threshold is at least
beta_i, so its A trace remains empty in volume. This includes an initially
supporting closed cut; any supporting trace has zero d-volume.

In particular L(u,v)>=0. On L>=0 the empty-cut inverse hinges vanish
because U_i=0, c_i>=0, and e_i>=0. Hence the finite lower-envelope
argument of Section 6 holds not only at the trial target but also at
the actual loss. For theta in the same finite set Theta put

    L_theta(p)=sum_i w_i^theta[dU_i+theta_i sigma_i c_i]/W_theta,
    J_theta(q)=sum_i w_i^theta theta_i sigma_i e_i/W_theta.

Then the actual optimized menu loss has the exact formula

    L(u,v)=max_(theta in Theta){u L_theta(p)+v J_theta(q)}.          (22)

Indeed the inverse sum on this range is
min_theta W_theta[L-uL_theta-vJ_theta]. At its actual zero every
branch is nonnegative and some branch is zero. This is exactly (22).
Thus for fixed actual centers the loss is convex, piecewise affine,
and positively homogeneous in the nonnegative rates. A maximizing
branch represents the required lower envelope; it is not an
independently assignable physical section allocation.

This also explains why a single proper-cut affine formula need not
survive the saturated case. The finite envelope, however, supplies
an exact replacement, consistent with the two tests in (13).
